questions.q: `pd.DataFrame.from_dict({'u1': {'age': 30}, 'u2': {'age': 41}}, orient='index')` produces what?
options: A single row with columns `u1.age` and `u2.age`
questions.why: `orient='index'` treats the outer keys as row labels and the inner keys as columns. The default (`orient='columns'`) would make `u1` and `u2` the columns.

questions.q: Which call gives the number of missing values in each column?
questions.why: `isna()` gives a boolean frame and summing it counts the `True` values per column. `count()` gives the **non**-missing counts; `axis=1` counts per row.

questions.q: `df.describe()` on a frame with numeric and string columns returns statistics for which columns by default?
options: It raises an error for mixed types
All columns, with NaN for strings
questions.why: By default `describe` summarises numeric columns. Pass `include='all'` or `include='object'` to describe the others.

questions.q: What does `df.dtypes.value_counts()` tell you?
options: How many rows have each dtype
How many columns have each dtype
The number of distinct values per column
questions.why: `df.dtypes` is a Series of one dtype per column, so counting its values groups the columns by type. `df.select_dtypes(include='number')` then selects one group.

questions.q: A column holds `['1', '2', 'n/a']`. What does `pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')` return?
questions.why: `errors='coerce'` turns unparseable entries into NaN, which forces a float dtype. The default `errors='raise'` would fail on `'n/a'`.

questions.q: You want to look up a column whose name might be `' Price '`, `'price'` or `'PRICE'`. Which approach is robust?
options: Compare `c.strip().lower()` for each name in `df.columns` with the wanted name
questions.why: Normalising both sides handles whitespace and case. `filter(like=...)` is case-sensitive and matches substrings, so it would also pick `'unit_price'` and miss `'PRICE'`.

questions.q: `pd.concat([df.head(2), df.tail(2)])` on a 3-row frame returns how many rows?
options: It raises because the index repeats
4, with the middle row appearing twice
questions.why: `head(2)` and `tail(2)` overlap on the middle row, and `concat` doesn't deduplicate. Check `len(df)` before previewing both ends.

questions.q: `df.info()` reports `Non-Null Count 980` for a column in a 1,000-row frame. What does that tell you?
options: 20 values in that column are missing
questions.why: `info()` shows the count of non-null entries per column alongside the dtype. Distinct values come from `nunique()`.

questions.q: After `df = df.sort_values('score')`, what does `df.loc[0]` return?
options: The row whose index **label** is 0, wherever it is now
An error, because the index is unsorted
The row with the lowest score, always
The first row of the sorted frame
questions.why: `loc` is label-based; sorting moves rows but keeps their labels. Use `df.iloc[0]` for the first position.

questions.q: Which filter is correct for rows where `a > 1` and `b == 'x'`?
questions.why: Element-wise logic needs `&` with parentheses (because `&` binds tighter than comparisons). Python's `and` tries to convert a whole Series to one boolean and raises `ValueError`.

questions.q: What does `df[['a', 'b']]` return compared with `df['a']`?
options: Two Series in a tuple, versus a DataFrame
A DataFrame with two columns, versus a Series
questions.why: A list of labels selects columns as a DataFrame; a single label returns a Series. `df[['a']]` returns a one-column DataFrame.

questions.q: `s1` has index `[a, b, c]` and `s2` has index `[b, c, d]`. What is `(s1 + s2).index`?
options: `[a, b, c, d]`, with NaN at `a` and `d`
questions.why: Arithmetic aligns on labels and takes the union; labels present on only one side produce NaN. Use `s1.add(s2, fill_value=0)` to treat missing as 0.

questions.q: You get `SettingWithCopyWarning` from `df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1`. What is happening?
options: The assignment may go to a temporary copy and leave `df` unchanged
questions.why: Chained indexing first produces a filtered frame (possibly a copy) and then assigns into it. `df.loc[df.x > 0, 'y'] = 1` does it in one step on `df` itself.

questions.q: After filtering rows and sorting, you want to keep each row's original position in the source frame. Which is simplest?
options: Keep the original index, or call `reset_index()` before filtering to store it as a column
Use `iloc` positions from the filtered frame
questions.why: Filtering and sorting preserve index labels, which are the original positions if the index was the default range. `drop=True` throws them away.

questions.q: `df.loc[2:4]` on a default integer index returns how many rows?
questions.why: Label slicing with `loc` includes both endpoints, unlike `iloc` and Python slices, which exclude the stop.

questions.q: To build a feature matrix in a fixed column order `cols`, which call raises if a column is missing?
questions.why: Selecting a missing label raises `KeyError`, which is what you want for a model's inputs. `reindex` silently adds NaN columns and `filter` silently drops missing ones.

questions.q: Per-station mean imputation: which line fills each NaN with its own station's mean?
questions.why: `transform` returns a value per original row, aligned to the frame, so `fillna` can use it directly. `groupby(...).mean()` returns one row per station, which doesn't align with the original rows.

questions.q: To keep the latest event per user, which is correct?
questions.why: After sorting by time ascending, the last occurrence for each user is the latest. Without sorting, `drop_duplicates` keeps whichever row happens to come first.

questions.q: What does `s.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(r'\s+', '_', regex=True)` do to `'  Total Revenue '`?
questions.why: Stripping first removes the outer spaces, lowering handles case, and replacing runs of whitespace gives single underscores.

questions.q: A survey column uses `-99` for "no answer". Which is the right cleaning step before computing a mean?
questions.why: Sentinel values are real numbers to pandas, so they pull the mean down until they are converted to NaN. `clip` would turn them into 0, which is still a wrong value.

questions.q: `df.dropna()` with no arguments drops which rows?
options: Only rows missing the first column
Only rows where every value is missing
Any row with at least one missing value
questions.why: The default is `how='any'` along rows. Use `how='all'` or `subset=[...]` to be less aggressive.

questions.q: You read CSV text into a frame with `pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))`. Why `StringIO`?
options: It converts the text to UTF-8
It is required for any header row
`read_csv` expects a path or file-like object, and `StringIO` wraps the string as a file
questions.why: Passing the raw string would be treated as a file path. `StringIO` gives the parser an in-memory file.

questions.q: `s.astype(int)` on a float column that contains NaN does what?
options: Leaves NaN as NaN in an int64 column
Raises, because NaN can't be an int; use the nullable `'Int64'` dtype
questions.why: NumPy integers have no missing value. Pandas' nullable `Int64` dtype (capital I) stores integers with `<NA>`.

questions.q: Which call standardises `'Yes'`, `'y'`, `'YES '` and `'no'` into booleans?
questions.why: Normalise first, then map the known spellings. `astype(bool)` makes every non-empty string `True`, including `'no'`.

questions.q: What is the difference between `groupby('g')['x'].transform('sum')` and `groupby('g')['x'].sum()`?
options: `transform` returns one value per original row; `sum` returns one per group
questions.why: `transform` broadcasts each group's result back to its rows, which is what you need for ratios like `x / group_total`.

questions.q: `df.groupby('team').agg(pts=('points', 'sum'), games=('game_id', 'nunique'))` returns what columns?
options: A MultiIndex of `(points, sum)` and `(game_id, nunique)`
One column per aggregation function name
questions.why: Named aggregation sets output column names directly and avoids the MultiIndex that `agg({'points': ['sum']})` creates.

questions.q: A pivot table of revenue by `region` × `quarter` with a total row and column uses which argument?
questions.why: `pivot_table(..., margins=True)` adds an `All` row and column using the same aggregation. `fill_value` only replaces empty cells.

questions.q: `pd.crosstab(y_true, y_pred)` produces what?
options: A table of counts with true labels as rows and predictions as columns
A table of proportions summing to 1
questions.why: `crosstab` counts co-occurrences, which for labels and predictions is the confusion matrix. `normalize='index'` gives per-class recall rows.

questions.q: To rank stores within each region by sales, which call is correct?
questions.why: A grouped `rank` restarts the ranking within each region and returns one rank per row. Sorting orders rows but doesn't produce ranks.

questions.q: What does `groupby('g').size()` count that `groupby('g')['x'].count()` doesn't?
questions.why: `size` counts every row in each group; `count` counts the non-null values of the column.

questions.q: By default, are rows with a NaN group key included in `groupby` results?
options: Yes, merged into the first group
Yes, as a group labelled NaN
No, they are dropped unless you pass `dropna=False`
questions.why: Missing keys are excluded by default, which can silently lose rows from totals. `dropna=False` keeps them as their own group.

questions.q: You compute `df.groupby('g')['x'].mean()` and the result index is `g`. Which call turns it back into a column?
questions.why: `reset_index` moves the group labels from the index into a regular column. `unstack` pivots an inner index level into columns.

questions.q: `orders.merge(users, on='user_id', how='left')` returns more rows than `orders` had. Why?
options: Merging always sorts and duplicates rows
Some orders have no matching user
questions.why: A left join keeps every left row and repeats it for each matching right row. Use `validate='many_to_one'` to catch duplicate keys early.

questions.q: Which merge keeps only rows whose key appears in both frames?
questions.why: Inner joins keep matches only. Left keeps all left rows, outer keeps everything, and cross makes every pair.

questions.q: `pd.concat([a, b])` where `b` has an extra column `z`. What happens?
options: The frames are joined side by side
The result has all columns; rows from `a` get NaN in `z`
It raises because the columns differ
questions.why: `concat` along rows takes the union of columns by default (`join='outer'`). `join='inner'` keeps only shared columns.

questions.q: A gradebook has columns `student, math, physics`. Which call makes it long with columns `student, subject, score`?
questions.why: `melt` unpivots the value columns into rows. `pivot` goes the other way, from long to wide.

questions.q: `long.pivot(index='step', columns='metric', values='value')` raises `ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries`. What does that mean?
options: Some `(step, metric)` pair appears more than once
questions.why: `pivot` needs a unique cell for each pair. Deduplicate first or use `pivot_table` with an aggregation.

questions.q: To start a new session whenever a user is idle for more than 30 minutes, which building block gives the time since the user's previous event?
questions.why: A grouped `diff` restarts at each user, so the first event of each user gets NaT instead of a gap from another user's event. Then `(gap > 30min).cumsum()` per user numbers the sessions.

questions.q: `merge(..., indicator=True)` adds which column?
options: `_merge`, saying whether each row came from left, right or both
The count of matches per key
questions.why: The indicator column is useful for anti-joins: `df[df._merge == 'left_only']` finds rows with no match.

questions.q: After `df.set_index(['a', 'b'])['v'].unstack()`, what becomes the columns?
questions.why: `unstack` moves the innermost index level (here `b`) into the columns, leaving `a` as the row index.
